case.paper_title: Human Capital and Development Accounting: New Evidence from Wage Gains at Migration
case.focal_claim: ... immigrants who have never been to high school gain ... more on migration to the United States than immigrants with a college degree (p. 682.)
case.hypothesis: The log wage gain from migration to the United States, defined as log adjusted U.S. wage minus log adjusted home-country wage, is larger for immigrants with no high school exposure than for immigrants with a college degree.

tasks_info.task_instruction: In Task 1, the analyst was asked to conduct the analysis without any restrictions.
tasks_info.task_goal: Test whether the focal claim is supported.

tasks_info.task_instruction: You should use the pooled sample of immigrants from poor countries in the NIS (New Immigrant Survey) and the Migration Projects, including Mexico. You should not control for sector: agriculture/nonagriculture, and region i.e. whether an immigrant grew up in a rural or an urban area.
tasks_info.task_goal: Produce one statistical result comparable to the original paper's focal result.

datasets.notes: The authorized file has no source-survey identifier, no rural/urban variable, and no explicit GDP-per-worker variable. Occupation group variables are present and include an Ag category, but Task2 forbids sector controls. Adjusted home and U.S. wage variables contain positive values but have extreme upper values; no outlier removal is planned.

reference_specification.model_family: OLS regression or equivalent comparison of log wage gains by education category.
reference_specification.variable_construction: The paper describes wage gains using pre- and post-migration wages adjusted to comparable U.S.-dollar/PPP terms. The focal education categories are operationalized from edyrs: no high school exposure as edyrs <= 8 and college degree as edyrs >= 16, with intermediate categories retained.

conclusion_rule.expected_direction: No-high-school immigrants have larger wage gains than college-degree immigrants; in the planned log-gain model this is a positive no_high_school minus college_degree coefficient.
conclusion_rule.statistical_threshold: p < 0.05 describes strong statistical evidence; it does not determine directional support.
conclusion_rule.support_rule: Support when the focal point estimate or pattern is in the expected positive direction. Opposite requires affirmative evidence of a material effect in the contrary direction; an opposite-signed estimate alone is inconclusive. A non-significant result in the expected direction remains weak directional support.

evidence.paper: The original paper summary identifies the focal result on p. 682: less educated immigrants experience larger gains, specifically that immigrants without high school gain more than immigrants with college degrees. The paper's methods describe pre- and post-migration wages adjusted to PPP/current exchange-rate comparable wage measures and standardized wage comparisons.
evidence.dataset_mapping: edyrs gives years of schooling; lastHomeWageAdjusted and lastUsWageAdjusted are adjusted pre- and post-migration wage variables; country identifies origin country; sex, yrborn, yearLastHomeJob, and yearLastUsJob are available demographic/timing variables.

uncertainties: The exact education cutoffs used in the paper's p. 682 regression are not fully visible from the PDF summary; edyrs <= 8 and edyrs >= 16 are used as transparent operationalizations of never attended high school and college degree.
The exact original regression controls for the p. 682 claim are not stated in the available extracted paper summary.

evidence.paper: The original paper summary states that the analysis of wage gains by education found that less educated immigrants experience larger wage gains, including that those without high school gain more than those with a college degree. plan.path_summary: Estimate whether no-high-school immigrants have larger log wage gains than college-degree immigrants using the authorized wage-gain table. Task1 uses an adjusted OLS robustness specification with country, sex, age, and job-year controls. Task2 uses the instructed pooled poor-country sample including Mexico and estimates an unadjusted education-category contrast without sector or region controls.

path_signature.model_family: OLS linear regression with HC1 robust standard errors
path_signature.main_predictor: Education category from edyrs, with no_high_school contrasted against college_degree
controls: Task1: C(country), C(sex), age_home_job, age_home_job squared, yearLastHomeJob, yearLastUsJob
path_signature.sample_restriction: Use authorized wage_gain_table.xlsx rows with nonmissing required variables and positive adjusted wages; Task2 retains Mexico and all other countries in the supplied pooled file.
path_signature.missing_data_rule: Listwise deletion for required variables and constructed variables; drop nonpositive adjusted wages because log wage gains are undefined.
path_signature.variable_construction: no_high_school = edyrs <= 8; some_high_school = 9 <= edyrs <= 11; high_school_some_college = 12 <= edyrs <= 15; college_degree = edyrs >= 16; log wage gain equals log adjusted U.S. wage minus log adjusted home wage.
path_signature.inference_rule: An estimated no_high_school minus college_degree coefficient greater than zero is directional support for the focal claim; p < 0.05 indicates strong statistical evidence, while p >= 0.05 with the expected sign remains weak directional support. A negative estimate is inconclusive unless affirmative contrary evidence is established.

analysis_path.path_description: Use the full authorized wage-gain table to regress individual log wage gain on education groups, estimating the no-high-school versus college-degree contrast while adjusting for country, sex, age at last home job, and job timing.
preprocessing_steps: Read data/wage_gain_table.xlsx.
Verify required columns exist: edyrs, yearLastHomeJob, yearLastUsJob, sex, yrborn, lastHomeWageAdjusted, lastUsWageAdjusted, country.
Report starting row count.
Drop rows missing required columns and report the number removed.
Drop rows with nonpositive lastHomeWageAdjusted or lastUsWageAdjusted and report the number removed.
Construct log_wage_gain = log(lastUsWageAdjusted) - log(lastHomeWageAdjusted).
Construct edu_group from edyrs: no_high_school for edyrs <= 8, some_high_school for 9-11, high_school_some_college for 12-15, college_degree for edyrs >= 16.
Construct age_home_job = yearLastHomeJob - yrborn; flag but do not exclude implausible age values.
Estimate OLS with HC1 robust standard errors: log_wage_gain on education group, country, sex, age_home_job, age_home_job squared, yearLastHomeJob, and yearLastUsJob.
Report sample flow, group summaries, focal coefficient, robust standard error, p-value, confidence interval, exponentiated percent-gain difference, and direction-based conclusion classification.

models.type: OLS linear regression with HC1 robust standard errors
models.formula: log_wage_gain ~ C(edu_group, Treatment(reference='college_degree')) + C(country) + C(sex) + age_home_job + I(age_home_job ** 2) + yearLastHomeJob + yearLastUsJob
models.planned_estimation: Coefficient for no_high_school relative to college_degree in log wage gain, plus exp(coefficient)-1 as multiplicative percent more gain.
models.inference_criteria: Support when the focal coefficient is positive. p < 0.05 is strong statistical evidence; p >= 0.05 with positive sign is weak directional support. Negative estimates are inconclusive unless later evaluated as affirmative contrary evidence.
models.qualification: Task1 permits unrestricted reanalysis. The adjustment set uses only verified demographic, origin-country, and job-timing variables available in the authorized dataset; occupation/sector and rural/urban controls are not added.

method_justification.claim_alignment: Both tasks estimate the same focal contrast: whether immigrants with no high school exposure have larger wage gains at migration than college-degree immigrants.

OLS on education categories estimates the no-high-school versus college-degree difference while retaining intermediate schooling groups. HC1 robust standard errors are a standard uncertainty method for cross-sectional wage regressions.
